title: Cache-namespace reshaping and stochastic TTL guardrail
creator: Anika Patel
description:
Objective: produce an automated recommendation engine and safe-apply workflow that reshapes cache namespaces (grouping/pivoting of prefix/key families) and applies per-namespace stochastic TTL schedules to maximize hit-rate lift while bounding cost and SLO risk. This ticket focuses on modeling, config generation, and a staged apply/rollback orchestrator with observable guardrails.

Problem context:
- Current prefix TTL tuning is manual and brittle: teams pick static TTLs which either waste cache memory or undercut hit-rate.
- Applying broad TTL changes has caused cost spikes or SLO regressions in past canaries.
- We need a way to (a) model expected hit-rate/cost tradeoffs per logical namespace, (b) synthesize safe TTL annealing schedules, and (c) roll changes out with automatic rollback triggers.

Deliverables:
- A hit-rate simulator for cache namespaces that ingests prefix telemetry (per-prefix QPS, miss/hit counts, token-length distribution) and outputs estimated delta in hit-rate, memory pressure, and per-token inference cost.
- A namespace reshaping heuristic: cluster prefixes into namespaces by access-pattern similarity (temporal locality, affix entropy, length distribution) and produce canonical keys for each namespace.
- Stochastic TTL generator: produces a schedule (initial TTL distribution, annealing steps, and sampling fraction) that can be applied incrementally to only a fraction of traffic to limit downside.
- Safe-apply orchestrator: rolling apply that supports shadowing, dry-run sampling, canary percentages, metric guardrails, and automated rollback on threshold breaches.
- Documentation and runbook for on-call and SRE (how to examine simulation outputs, adjust safety thresholds, and run emergency rollbacks).
acceptance_criteria: Simulator validated on historical traffic from two production routes with estimated hit-rate within 5% of observed after replay
Namespace clustering produces stable clusters (adjusted rand index > 0.6 against manual labels) for >80% of sampled buckets
Staged apply supports 0 -> 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% rollout with automatic rollback if miss-rate increases >3 p.p. or latency P95 increases >10%
Automated rollback completes within 2 minutes of threshold detection and is instrumented in the console with a single-click manual override
Runbook and short technical note published in Confluence with links to simulation notebook and sample configs
plan: 1) Data scaffold: assemble per-prefix telemetry (1 month) and build a replay harness for offline simulator. 2) Modeling: implement a Bayesian hit-rate bootstrap that estimates marginal benefit of increasing TTL per namespace, accounting for overlap and cache size. 3) Namespace reshaping: K-means + suffix/affix hashing hybrid to avoid pathological splits. 4) Stochastic TTL synth: design sampling-aware TTL distributions and annealing steps that reduce variance when scaled. 5) Orchestrator: implement staged apply with shadow mode, metrics hooks, and rollback policies. 6) Validation: two route canaries (internal and customer sandbox) and one low-risk production for final verification. 7) Docs/runbook and handover to SRE.
rollout_plan:
- Phase 0 (dry-run): simulate on last 28 days of traffic in notebook; produce candidate namespace configs and expected deltas.
- Phase 1 (shadow): apply TTL sampling with 1% of traffic in shadow mode (no effect on cache state) for 48h.
- Phase 2 (canary): apply stochastic TTL to 1% real traffic for 12h, then 5% for 24h, monitor guardrails.
- Phase 3 (ramp): increase to 25% for 6h then 100% if no triggers.
- Rollback criteria: miss-rate delta > +3 percentage points AND downstream token cost reduction < 1% (indicates harmful cache misses), OR latency P95 regression > 10% sustained for 10m, OR error-rate increase > 0.5 p.p.
- Emergency rollback: immediate stop and revert to previous TTLs; automated revert job removes staged keys and signals SRE channel.
monitoring: Metrics to track: per-namespace hit-rate, miss-rate, cache occupancy (bytes & entries), median and P95 latency, token cost per minute, error rate, and modelled expected hit uplift from simulator. Dashboards: create a per-release dashboard in Console with delta vs baseline, and an alert rule for rollback triggers. Logs: record applied TTL policy id and namespace id on every request path for postmortem.
safety_gates:
- Shadow mode for sim-to-prod validation.
- Sampled rollout with stochastic assignment so the first customers see small random subsets before larger scale.
- Soft thresholds (warnings) followed by hard thresholds (auto-rollback) for miss-rate, latency, and cost spikes.
- Canary isolation: canary traffic routed to dedicated serving nodes to limit cross-impact with global caches.
- Backfill guard: detect sudden increases in hotkey churn and pause rollouts if backfill CPU for serving nodes > 60%.
implementation_notes: Modeling approach: use hierarchical Bayesian model per-namespace with a Poisson-Gamma observation model for hits/misses and a prior informed by historical seasonality. Use reservoir sampling to keep bounded memory when training over long tails. Namespace clustering: feature vector = [30m autocorr, top-10 suffix entropy, median token length, 95th-percentile request interarrival]. TTL schedule: expressive form is a mixture of discrete TTL buckets plus probability mass for sampling new keys (stochastic TTL).
experiments: Offline replay against route 'chat-gen-v2' showed potential 12% hit-rate uplift for 10% more cache memory with conservative TTL anneal
Shadow run on 'embed-search' 2026-02-12 produced stable simulated-to-observed error within 4% across 48h window
Prototype namespace clustering reduced key cardinality by 18% when canonicalizing similar affixes
risks_and_mitigation: Risk: Mis-clustering hotkeys causes regression for a small set of high-value customers -> Mitigation: exclude top-100 keys per route from automatic reshaping and require manual opt-in.

Risk: Batch windows interact poorly with stochastic sampling and inflate latency -> Mitigation: add a compatibility filter that prevents TTL sample traffic from being batched beyond configured window and monitor P95 delta separately.
Risk: Memory pressure unexpected -> Mitigation: simulator predicts byte impact; orchestrator enforces a soft memory ceiling and pauses rollout if projected occupancy > 85%.
Risk: Edge cases with streaming sessions where prefix grows over time -> Mitigation: tag session prefixes and apply session-aware TTL rules (shorter decay) rather than blanket namespace TTLs.
